The 7 Best Blue Light Glasses of 2026, Out Of the 24 Pairs We Tested

These glasses effectively filter blue light, reduce glare, and provide comfort for all-day wear.

Updated on July 03, 2026
By Jaylyn Pruitt Jaylyn is a Health associate editor who tested blue light glasses and spoke to optometrists to find out how to reduce eye strain.

Whether you have a vision impairment that requires a prescription or not, blue light blocking may be useful if you experience eye strain. Blue light is everywhere, from our digital screens to the natural sunshine. And while blue light has some benefits—such as increasing alertness and elevating mood1—the negative side effects can include eye strain, dry eyes, headaches, and difficulty sleeping, according to a study from the University of California, Davis.

To determine which blue light glasses work the best, we tested 24 pairs at home for a week and evaluated each pair for fit, feel, clarity, effectiveness, and value. The best blue light glasses can help alleviate eye strain from increased blue light exposure and counteract its suppressive effect on the release of melatonin (the hormone that signals to your brain that it’s time to sleep). However, experts say evidence on the effectiveness of blue light glasses is mixed. So, be sure to take 20-minute screen breaks and adjust your brightness settings at night to reduce stress on your eyes, even if you’re using blue light glasses.

The Benicci Blue Light Glasses impressed us with their lightweight design and wearability. Our editor, who never wears glasses, said she barely noticed these glasses on her face because they were so light, making it easy to transition to daily wear. And while they’re lightweight, they’re incredibly durable. Even though we tugged and pulled on them to test their durability, they felt almost indestructible.

Our Testing Process

To find the most effective blue light eye protection, we spent over 300 hours testing 24 pairs of blue light glasses. We began our test by working for four hours without wearing blue light glasses and noted any eye pain or discomfort experienced. In the second half of the workday, we tested a pair of blue light glasses for four hours and noted how our eyes felt after wearing them. Following this initial test, we wore each pair of blue light glasses for a week, working and interacting with screens as usual. We assessed each pair based on the following factors:

Fit: We noted how well the glasses stayed in place while wearing them and if they were comfortable for extended use. We also looked at adjustments and whether it was challenging to get a good fit, and if adjustments were needed frequently.
Feel: We evaluated the comfort of the glasses, the flex of the arms, and their ability to contour smoothly to the face. We also considered whether they were lightweight and comfortable or heavy and burdensome, and if there were any marks or discomfort after extended wear.
Clarity: We observed the clarity of the lenses and the clarity of our vision while looking through the lenses, noting any distortions or blurriness.
Effectiveness: We noted whether they successfully reduced eye strain and fatigue when working in front of a screen for hours.
Value: We considered whether the price was justified based on the glasses’ overall performance and whether we would use the glasses regularly or recommend them to others.
Our Experts


We consulted with five eyecare experts for their professional advice regarding what to look for when selecting the best blue light glasses. The experts we spoke to included:

Dora Adamopoulos, OD, Medical Advisor to The Vision Council
Mark Fromer, M.D., a New York-based ophthalmologist at the Manhattan Eye, Ear, and Throat Hospital
Bradley Katz, MD, PhD, a neuro-ophthalmologist at the University of Utah’s Moran Eye Center and CEO of Axon Optics
Dagny Zhu, MD, an ophthalmologist and expert at myvision.org
James Dello Russo, OD, a LASIK surgeon and ophthalmologist at the New Jersey Eye Care Center

What to Look For When Shopping for Blue Light Glasses

Fit: Eyeglasses should be lightweight, fit snugly on the nose, and have non-slip nose and temple pads to keep them in place.
Lens Coatings: Opt for lenses with anti-glare, anti-reflective, and scratch-resistant coatings for better clarity and durability. Some blue light glasses also offer UV protection.
Tint: The level of tint affects how much blue light is filtered. Yellow or amber-tinted lenses block more blue light, which is great for heavy screen use in the evening. Clear lenses with minimal tint offer basic blue light protection.
Prescriptions: If you wear prescription glasses, look for brands that offer blue light filtering lenses with prescription capabilities.
Style: The specific style of glasses, such as wire or plastic frames, does not affect their ability to block blue light. However, consider a pair with larger lenses to block more blue light.
Effectiveness: If you’d like to know exactly how much blue light your glasses block, you can ask the manufacturer for the transmittance spectrum report. For an at-home test, hold your glasses up to a light source; if the light reflection on the lens appears blue, it will likely block some percentage of blue light, recommends James Dello Russo, OD, a LASIK surgeon and ophthalmologist at the New Jersey Eye Care Center.
